newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese prosecutors seek help in copper scandal.
newsitem.headline: Japanese prosecutors seek help in copper scandal.

text.p: Japanese prosecutors are seeking help from local trade houses in their probe into Sumitomo Corp's $2.6 billion copper trading loss, sources close to the case said on Tuesday.

The Tokyo District Public Prosecutor's Office, which set up a special task force last month to probe the copper scandal, is interviewing local metal traders about the workings of the London Metal Exchange (LME), they said.
The firms, asked by Japanese prosecutors to help their probe into the biggest financial loss in history, include Mitsui & Co Ltd, according to the sources.

"The specialist team (of the Tokyo prosecutor's office) recently met a senior Mitsui metal trader and asked him detailed questions about the mechanisms of how the LME copper contract is traded," one source said.
Sumitomo Corp originally announced in June that it had suffered $1.8 billion in losses from unauthorised copper trades, and blamed the long-time head of its copper trading division Yasuo Hamanaka.
It revised the figure on September 19, saying the losses had soared to $2.6 billion.
Hamanaka, 48, a veteran trader once dubbed "Mr Five Percent" since his trading team was believed to control five percent of world copper trade, was fired in June.

Sumitomo said Hamanaka had deceived the company for about a decade while his losses snowballed as he tried to cover an initial 6.5 billion yen ($58.5 million) off-the-books loss with more secret trades.
So far no criminal charges have been brought in the case.

Sumitomo announced last month that it had decided to press for criminal charges against Hamanaka, but a spokesman for the firm said on Tuesday that it had not made a decision as to when to submit a criminal complaint against him to prosecutors.
Hamanaka has declined to comment on the losses.
The Tokyo prosecutor's office has already questioned some metal traders at Sumitomo with close ties with Hamanaka, the sources close to the case said.
They said Mitsui carried out a detailed investigation into Hamanaka's trading patterns several years ago.
"Mitsui traders were so irritated with Hamanaka's trading performance and high profile in the market, they tried to find out what his magic was," a source close to Mitsui said.
"I heard later they failed to find out what Hamanaka was doing, but their research data will give the prosecutor's office some important clues," the source said.
Mitsui & Co spokesman Takamichi Shinoda said the firm constantly studies the trading methods of other trade houses, but refused to comment on whether the company was helping prosecutors.
"It's not a surprise that we studied Sumitomo's metal trading, but we can't answer that question," he said.
A Mitsubishi Corp spokesman denied a rumour that the company was cooperating with prosecutors.
Sumitomo is conducting its own in-house investigation with a 60-strong task force sifting through 2,000 boxes of documents.
Company president Kenji Miyahara last month accused Hamanaka of conducting as many as 2,000 unauthorised deals in a single year and of forging documents to cover his tracks. ($1=111 yen)
